chunks: "PVT stands for process, voltage and temperature, the three things that make a chip's real behavior differ from its nominal design.
Process is manufacturing variation: no two dies are identical.
Threshold voltage, gate length, oxide thickness and wire dimensions vary from lot to lot, wafer to wafer, and across a die.
Fast silicon has lower thresholds and gives more drive current, so higher frequency, but it also leaks much more. Slow silicon is the opposite.
Voltage is the supply seen at the transistors. It differs from the setpoint because of regulator tolerance, IR drop and transient droop.
Higher voltage means faster but more dynamic power, as V squared, and more leakage. Lower voltage saves power but can break timing.
Temperature changes carrier mobility, threshold voltage and leakage.
Hot silicon usually has lower mobility, so it is slower at normal voltages, and leakage rises roughly exponentially, doubling every 10 to 20 degrees or so.
At advanced nodes and low voltages there can be temperature inversion where cold is the slow case.
So design and test have to cover the corners: slowest process at low voltage for setup timing, fastest at high voltage for hold, and fast and hot for worst-case leakage and power.
Then we use guardbanding, binning and on-die sensors with adaptive voltage scaling to turn that variation into a spec."
